newsitem.title: UK: Oil slumps under $19 a barrel as supply surges.
newsitem.headline: Oil slumps under $19 a barrel as supply surges.

text.p: World oil prices tumbled to their lowest level in seven months on Friday, undermined by traders' perceptions that growing supply bolstered by rising Iraqi exports is outstripping demand.

Bellwether North Sea Brent finished down 50 cents at $18.85 a barrel, the first time the benchmark crude has traded under the psychologically important $19 level since August 1, when it posted a low of $18.79.
Brent has fallen 94 cents in a week, extending a 20 percent slide from just below $25 a barrel in early January.

Traders believe rising output will continue to outpace oil requirements in the gap between the two main seasons of consumer demand -- heating oil in winter and gasoline for increased car use in the northern hemisphere summer.

"I think the market's got the potential to go a lot lower," said Nauman Barakat at brokers Prudential Bache. "Sentiment is still bearish on heating oil and crude and there's no concern yet about tightness in gasoline."
"Refiners in the U.S. and Europe are in maintenance, the mild weather has hit heating oil demand and gasoline looks OK," said a trader.
Friday's fall was accelerated by U.S. traders aggressively selling U.S. crudes lower to reflect weakness in the prices of American gasoline and heating oil.
"The whole market lacks confidence at the moment so the bounce (back above $19) on Monday may not be that strong," one trader said
Rising Iraqi exports under the United Nations' oil-for-food exchange remained at the centre of market concern.
Iraq has signed contracts for half a dozen extra spot cargoes in an effort to make up for a shortfall in revenue from contract sales under the U.N. deal.
Baghdad is allowed to sell oil to the value of $1 billion in the 90 days to March and another one billion dollars' worth by June 9.
Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) was looking for another spot buyer in the oversupplied Mediterranean market on Friday, traders said.
Dealers said the Iraqi crude has been sold at discounts to the value fixed by the U.N. for sales by SOMO, making the crude difficult to shift.
The U.N. is expected to renew the oil sale, designed to offset the impact of sanctions imposed after Iraq's invasion of Kuwati, for a second six months.
Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said on Friday Baghdad would approach the organisation for permission to increase the $2 billion ceiling.
But a diplomat at the U.N. familar with the deal said any increase was unlikely.
